speaker: The Chairman
text: You can just take the first cut alone.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Chairman, can I take all my five cuts together?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Just one, please, and then I will call on the subsequent four.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head S of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: In my five cuts, I wish to highlight five groups of workers in Singapore whom I am concerned about and wish to speak up for.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Fourth, those who have special needs and fifth, those who are ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: The workforce profile in Singapore is changing rapidly.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Last year during the Debate on the President's Address, the Minister shared that the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) will step up support for mid-career jobseekers and the long-term unemployed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Till today, there are mature PMETs who have shared their difficulties and challenges in finding and landing in jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Have we been successful thus far in assisting these groups of workers?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: The new Career Trial will also enable more jobseekers to try out short-term work stints to facilitate their assessment of new jobs and careers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Can MOM provide an update on these programmes and their efficacy in minimising job mismatches?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: In addition, for those who have been successfully placed, how have the retention rates been in the past one year?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: The Minister also shared last year that MOM will also transform its employment services through technology.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: The "MyCareersFuture" portal will make job searches more personalised, smarter and faster to better help jobseekers and employers find suitable matches.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Can MOM provide an update on how far this portal has been effective in reducing missed matches and getting more Singaporeans into quality jobs?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Patrick Tay, I understand you have woven all the five cuts into one speech.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I have also met young PMETs who themselves have faced challenges in securing a job.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: The Career Starter Programme was first announced in May 2018.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Can MOM share how the programme benefits graduating students?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Then, there is the issue of underemployment of PMETs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: However, I am more concerned about non-time-based underemployment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: This is where PMETs do "smaller" and "lesser" jobs than what they are equipped, trained or competent for.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I have been speaking about this the past few years and I recommend a comprehensive study to ascertain the severity of this amongst PMETs in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: PME union representation is something that the Labour Movement has been pushing for.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: The Industrial Relations Act was amended in 2015 to permit rank-and-file unions to collectively represent executive employees.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: In order to avoid conflicts of interest and undermining management effectiveness, executives with senior management functions were excluded from collective representation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: These functions are set out in section 17(3) of the Act.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: The tripartite partners have also issued the Tripartite Guidelines on Extending the Scope of Union Representation for Executives.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: On the ground, our unions have come across instances where employers cite section 17(3) to deny collective representation for executives who are not really in senior management grades or having access to information which would give rise to a genuine conflict of interest if they should be represented by the union.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Patrick Tay, do not worry about the timing.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We will add in another four minutes when you hit zero.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Some examples are, first, employees, such as sales executives or engineers who help to prepare project bids.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: We have come across cases where employers have refused to allow union representation simply because these employees have access to confidential information on the company's budget and finances.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Second, executives who carry out the initial rounds of performance appraisals of employees whom they are supervising, though they do not make the final determination of the employee's performance grade or promotion.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Employers have sometimes argued that such executives are not entitled to collective representation because they can influence decisions on other employees' performance.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: This will help employers and unions to reach a consensus on the extension of scope smoothly and expeditiously.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Considering the above issues and challenges faced by PMETs in Singapore, I suggest the tripartite partners should work together to examine in detail the plight of PMETs in Singapore, the precarious and vulnerable PMETs, so that we can identify any blind spots and further strengthen our efforts to pre-emptively and proactively assist them.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I have been lobbying on strengthening the Singaporean Core, Fair and Progressive Hiring and the eradication of nationality bias since 2011.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: It has been an arduous but positive journey.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: We have seen the introduction of the Fair Consideration Framework (FCF) and the National Jobs Bank in 2014.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: There are also greater focus and awareness of the move towards not just fair but progressive workplaces and employment practices.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Anecdotally, the situation has improved when I speak to fellow PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: However, in this regard, I do still hear complaints that employment agencies and placement companies are also where some of these malpractices and nationality discrimination happen.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: In some cases, the nationality discrimination results in job losses of local PMEs and the hiring of foreign PMEs for jobs which local PMEs can fill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: MOM had also introduced the Capability Transfer Programme last year.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: This was to help and support the transfer of specialised knowledge to strengthen the Singaporean Core of talents for the future.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Another form of discrimination is with respect to age, ageism, as they call it.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I have raised this at the Ministry of Law's Committee of Supply (COS), but I am raising this again, as anecdotally, harassment in the workplace, whether sexual or non-sexual in nature, is something that cannot be condoned or tolerated.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Currently, we have a tripartite advisory and legislation, such as the Protection from Harassment Act and the Penal Code, which already empower the Police and the Courts to deal with egregious cases of harassment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: For cases of workplace harassment that do not cross the threshold to constitute a criminal offence, it is still important that they are managed well.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: How can we provide more support to employers and employees to do so?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: How can we ensure those who whistleblow are not prejudiced against?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Another group of workers and jobseekers I am concerned about are those with special needs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Beyond those with disabilities, there are those with special needs, such as autism and attention deficit hyperactive disorder, attention deficit disorder, dyslexia and other medical and mental conditions, such as depression.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: We know many countries in the West have strong support systems and ecosystems to provide meaningful work and jobs for such jobseekers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Can we study their successes so that we can build a similarly strong system and framework here in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I am aware the Open Door Programme supports companies to hire, train and integrate persons with special needs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: How can we build on these efforts to help more persons with special needs to join the workforce?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: The final group is those who are ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I am aware the Singapore Corporation of Rehabilitative Enterprises (SCORE) has been doing more to help their inmates transit and reintegrate back into society when they are released.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Ex-offenders may require more help to reintegrate back in society, including finding employment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: This includes those who are on tagged and on day release.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: How are we helping ex-offenders re-enter and remain in employment?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: (In Mandarin):   I would like to call for more attention to be paid to five groups of vulnerable workers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I urge the tripartite partners to strengthen collaboration, understand the various needs of vulnerable PMETs and provide timely and effective assistance to these workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Fourth, we should also pay attention to workers with special needs and give them opportunities to realise their potential.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It can range from insensitive comments from a colleague on a working mother's maternity leave to ageism, to abusive remarks by customers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It can happen to any worker, regardless of age, gender, race, industry or job function.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Whatever the form and whoever the target, it causes distress and exerts an undue toll on our workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It has no place in our modern workplace.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must first improve the awareness among victims and provide channels for them to seek assistance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is important that we educate both employers and employees on how to respond to workplace abuse and harassment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must make unambiguous that there are clear lines that cannot be crossed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In addition, for those who might be affected by workplace harassment, we can consider counselling, especially for our frontline workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, counselling was introduced in National University Hospital.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is a free and confidential service that has been very useful for the healthcare professionals who work in a high-stress environment amidst high service expectations by the public and patients.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Such services can be useful to help employees cope with their workplace stresses better.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They have sent out many job applications but receive minimal responses or just rejection letters.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Being unemployed not only affects a person’s financial commitments and his ability to pay the bills for housing and food, it also affects their self-confidence because they are unable to earn a fair income to support or contribute to the family.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is even more difficult if the person who has lost the job is above 50 or 55 years.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many times, they blame the human resource (HR) departments of the hiring companies for not even considering them for an interview once their age is disclosed.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Some of these residents have put the blame on foreigners and assert that their job losses are caused by foreigners who have displaced them.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I went into MyCareersFuture recently and found that there are 24,268 jobs available.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But yet from the experience of my residents, it seems that it is really not so easy to find a job among those over 24,000 available jobs.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Has MOM carried out any survey to assess whether jobseekers are aware of the role of the Government agencies in helping them to find alternative jobs?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: How else can we persuade jobseekers that if they can make some adjustments to their expectations, it would be easier for them to find alternative employment?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Last year, I raised a concern about the many companies that are on the FCF watchlist.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Does MOM still receive feedback about companies where almost every worker is a foreigner and what other actions can MOM take to signal our unhappiness with such companies and to discourage them from discriminating against employing Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Lastly, it is about seniors above 67 years old.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Does MOM monitor the statistics about seniors who have retired after 65 to 67 but are still active and willing to work but were asked to retire because of their age?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: What else can we do about such seniors who are still healthy and capable of contributing to the workforce?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I know of companies which say that they have to keep an eye on their headcount and, hence, have to let these seniors retire even though they can still contribute to the company.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Chairman, in the last few years, we have heard this phrase "Jobs-skills Mismatch" being used to explain the discrepancies between the share of jobseekers and job openings in the labour market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have also heard this phrase being used to frame retraining and reskilling policies and nudge workers to reskill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As Industry 4.0 looms and new cyber-physical system threatens to replace workers, the phrase has taken on a greater sense of anxiety.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am not suggesting that jobs-skills mismatch does not exist and the phrase has been misused.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My concern is that without proper study, the concept becomes the presumption rather than fact, an ideology rather the truth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our workers will waste their time going down blind alleys.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This means that our workers are not over-educated, demanding of high pay and lacking experience.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are a few things that we can learn from this study.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, employers seem to be more concerned about specific skills than generic skills.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a concern as employers should not be looking for narrowly specific skills.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second, the MCF platform may be inadvertently promoting non-generic skills mismatches by allowing for fine grain skills-based job searches.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One interesting finding of the study is that the persistence of workers in applying for jobs and the greater activity of employers on the MCF platform improved application outcomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The conclusion may well be that, at this juncture, the Government should do less in applying technological solutions and focus on nudging workers and employers to do more to close the gap between jobs and skills.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, with the technological shift, we see new opportunities, but it also requires businesses and people to adapt and change in order to be able to take advantage of the opportunities and deal with the disruptions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What is most challenging is the speed of change we are experiencing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Much of the disruption to jobs are being driven by technological changes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: New opportunities are created with these disruptions, but they do require new skills and mindsets to take on these new roles.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Hence, it is no longer about providing quality jobs but also providing the support and development for employees so that they are ready for these new jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the trends I have just described, it means that people need to build capabilities throughout their lives and careers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Businesses, too, need to adapt to the changes of the market to effectively develop the capabilities of their people across different age groups and segments and to access talent.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Across the several agencies – WorkForce Singapore (WSG), SkillsFuture Singapore, e2i, the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC), the Infocomm Media Development Authority and many more – there are numerous programmes and initiatives to support individuals and organisations build capability for the new economy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How can these efforts be better leveraged effectively to match people to the right programmes and organisations to the capabilities they need?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How has WSG helped mature PMET jobseekers and those who have been unemployed for long periods?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can MOM share how the A&G initiative and growth sector efforts help jobseekers take up new jobs?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How effective has the A&G initiatives been and what are the new jobs that PMET jobseekers and those who been unemployed for some time taken on with the initiative?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What is MOM’s assessment of the success of the programme so far?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Have our Singaporean PMETs whose jobs have been disrupted been able to adapt and take advantage of the new job opportunities?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, underemployment basically refers to situations where a person is working but below capacity.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In a 2017 survey on underemployment by the Ong Teng Cheong Institute (OTC Institute), it was found that underemployed persons tend to face many challenges, such as low morale, insecurity about their job and income, and difficulties in meeting daily expenses.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While we are responding to job disruption by engaging in economic transformation and reskilling workers, it would be wishful thinking to expect that displaced workers would find work in new industries in a seamless manner and without any discontinuity in income and benefits.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, it would be most useful to know how well the professional conversion programmes, such as A&G, did in terms of matching jobseekers with new jobs of comparable pay, or the extent of the pay cuts taken.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Further, I understand that A&G consists of two sub-schemes: Place and Train, where an employer has been found for the jobseeker, and Attach and Train, where training is done before an employer is found.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For this latter group under Attach and Train, what was the success rate for placements?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Currently, MOM presents underemployment based solely on time, that is, those working part-time when they wished to work additional hours.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While this is an internationally accepted indicator, the International Labour Organisation has, over the years, highlighted the multifaceted nature of underemployment that cannot be captured by time alone.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, in 1998, it passed a resolution stating that there was a need to revise the existing standards on the measurement of underemployment and to broaden the scope to include also inadequate employment situations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Inadequate employment situations cover all those in employment who want to change their current work situation for reasons, such as inadequate use and mismatch of occupational skills; inadequate income; working excessive hours or in unstable jobs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Broadly speaking, inadequate employment could be skills-related, income-related or working excessive hours.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, the OTC Institute survey mentioned earlier recognised that underemployment was too complex to be measured by a single factor alone, for example, time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In view of all these, can MOM update the House on its tracking of, and policy towards, underemployment?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These include food services, retail and real estate, amongst others, while other sectors, such as construction, do not have any manpower targets as their manpower needs are seasonal and based on cyclical factors.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At the recent pre-Budget dialogue with the Institute of Chartered Accountants, some panelists stated that they only had a vague idea of how SMEs stand to benefit from the ITMs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How do the ITMs support these objectives, and can they play a more facilitative role in this regard than is currently the case, particularly for smaller SMEs that may find it more challenging to take advantage of the ITM format to fulfil the larger national objectives of creating a strong and united Singapore?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Mr Chairman, technological advancements and disruptions, together with the gig economy, are changing the way organisations structure work.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Today's gig economy does have experienced, talented people who possess deep skills and prefer independent work.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: These workers often choose to enter the gig economy rather than the traditional workforce in order to have more autonomy and ownership over their work, as well as flexibility over their schedules.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: More people may be choosing freelancing as their primary job because they have multiple skills, which allow them to fill up their time with different types of jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Due to the relatively low barriers to entry, there are also individuals who may decide against seeking formal employment and choose to be self-employed as an alternative to generate income in order to be self-sufficient or in times when they have difficulties finding suitable employment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The profile of SEPs in Singapore is diverse, with many different occupations.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: While many chose flexible freelance work that fits their lifestyle, they are sacrificing job security, perks and benefits.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: There is a growing concern as to whether there is adequate support for their long-term financial, healthcare and retirement needs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: SEPs may not be able to raise their fees as it may make them uncompetitive when they bid for assignments.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Hence, it may make it hard to keep up with the cost of living.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: There are growing instances of SEPs that are not paid on time, accurately and, in some cases, not paid at all for work done.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: They lack protection against loss of income from prolonged illness or injury and do not have sick leave or health benefits.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Some insurance policies do include such a rider, but there are no such standalone insurance products.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: SEPs are also challenged in developing their skills to stay current, given the near-term demands of being self-employed.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Could the Ministry also look into more ways to encourage gig workers to make further voluntary contributions to other accounts of their CPF by providing them with strong incentives to do so?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: There is substantial evidence from public policy efforts that positive actions can be induced through non-compulsory incentive mechanisms.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: For instance, could a "default" be established where CPF deductions, beyond MediSave, initially match those of regular-economy workers with the same job profile, but being non-binding, would permit opting into a lower amount?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Alternatively, could gig workers receive information in their CPF statements about typical contributions by regular-economy workers in comparable employment circumstances, to encourage them to follow the "social norm"?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: SEPs typically face short-term cash flow needs, which may trump their longer-term economic interest in saving for future retirement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But CPF payouts only form part of retirement income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The self-employed, caregivers and homemakers do not contribute to CPF and rely on private savings for retirement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Older generations were especially likely to have low CPF savings, because self-employment and informal work were more common.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: As for women, in 1990, about half of working-age women were out of the labour force and, even today, about one in four are out.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Going forward, can we ensure that CPF becomes the basic retirement system even for the self-employed, caregivers and homemakers?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: First, technological disruption is likely to increase the extent of self-employment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While about one in 10 today are self-employed, this may increase in the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Even a few years spent out of regular employment will have significant impact on CPF savings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Divorce rates have risen rapidly, and this has affected older women.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Many women have spent substantial time out of work to take care of their family.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There are also fewer children to provide support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Women have no statutory entitlements to retirement assets in divorce or widowhood.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It depends on whether the Court orders distribution of CPF in a divorce, and also whether the deceased names the widow as the nominee for CPF.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Statutory entitlements for divorcees and widows do exist elsewhere.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In the United States, divorced spouses have entitlements to their ex-spouse's social security, and in the United Kingdom (UK), spouses who are caregivers earn credits towards their state pension.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What has the Ministry observed about the extent to which current and projected retirement gaps exist for own account workers and caregivers?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What is the work done on policies that address these gaps, such as mandatory contributions to the RAs for own account workers, matching credits to CPF, and entitlements for caregivers and homemakers based on Government credits, or from spousal accounts?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, the last move of the retirement age to 62 and the re-employment age to 67 was made in 2017.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Since then, there have been calls to review the next steps in promoting the employment of older workers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I understand that there is an ongoing review of the retirement and re-employment ages.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can MOM share the progress of this review and whether any outcome has been arrived at?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In our Parliament Sitting in February this year, we passed the combined Motions on the elderly and caregiving.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my speech in support of that Motion, I urged MOM to consider raising the CPF contribution rates for Singaporeans aged 55 and above, something which I had spoken about in this Chamber before.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even if the CPF contribution rate is to be cut, it should be done progressively over several years, rather than a drastic 11% cut as you cross your 55th birthday.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As more Singaporeans are marrying and having children later, at age 55, many would still be servicing their housing mortgages, supporting school-going children as well as elderly parents.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I recognise that the lower CPF contribution rates for older workers help them to remain employable, the reality is that there is already a tradeoff in terms of having saved up enough for retirement and in fulfilling their financial commitments towards housing, education and caregiving for elderly parents.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At 55, many Singaporeans would still be economically active.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Restored CPF contribution rates will help in paying housing loans, education or tuition fees for their children, and additional medical expenses for elderly parents.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Is there scope to revise upwards the CPF contribution rates of older workers aged 55 and above while at the same time maintaining their employability?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Increasingly, seniors are expressing an interest in continuing to work for a variety of reasons, such as to continue to earn an income, to keep their minds and bodies active, to stay engaged in the workplace and community or simply because they enjoy their vocations.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is no reason why they should be forced to retire just because they have reached a cut-off age.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I understand that the relevance of the retirement and re-employment age concept has been relooked.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would MOM share if any conclusion has been reached?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Older workers have lower CPF contribution rates today to keep their total remuneration competitive and help them remain employable.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The tradeoff is that they will have less to save up for their retirement.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, we are also seeing improvements in older workers' employability and longer life expectancies.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Their wealth of experience, cumulative knowledge and skillsets are assets, enabling them to make valuable contributions to their work.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope that we can help them to attract more contributions to their CPF, so that they can enjoy a more secure retirement.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is there scope to revise the CPF contribution rates of older workers while at the same time maintaining their employability?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Older workers have a lot to contribute but their physical decline with age is expected.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Redesigning job environments and functions will allow our seniors to continue working smoothly.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is the Ministry’s assessment of how rapidly our businesses are redesigning jobs to make workplaces more age-friendly?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am especially concerned about senior workers in menial jobs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Does MOM have measures to get employers to expedite job redesign and create better work conditions so that the work is less strenuous for elder workers?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are there plans to update or refine the WorkPro scheme?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Does MOM have data on the number and profile of companies which offer FWAs and the number of employees who take it up?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How many companies have tapped on the Enhanced Work-Life Grant and how many employees have benefited?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would MOM provide a breakdown on how many organisations have utilised the FWA Incentive and Job Sharing Incentive?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How can we encourage even more companies to offer FWAs?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Removing the retirement age not only removes the first expiry date but also changes the current notion about the expiry of work abilities that is fixed by age.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The re-employment age should also be redefined so that it is not referring to another expiry date but to a transition at age 70.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: This transition obliges employers to put our senior workers on rolling contracts on the same terms that should go on without an expiry date as long as the workers are still able and productive and want to work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: It is the transition that allows employer and employee to evaluate performance and productive levels together, work out flexible work contracts if the employee so wishes and collaborate on job and workplace redesign to keep up productivity.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I wish to speak about the financial security of Singaporeans aged 65 and above.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This generation worked hard to lay the foundation of the Singapore we enjoy today.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: During their time, wages were low and many worked in the informal sector.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These payouts are clearly insufficient to provide for today's cost of living.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many of these seniors rely heavily on family support for financial security.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The majority cited "allowances from children' as their main source of income.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, I am concerned about this generation's over-reliance on their children, what with the shrinking size of families and the consequent burden that it will have on the shoulders of the younger generation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I greatly appreciate the launch of the Silver Support Scheme to supplement seniors' retirement incomes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But I always wonder if the amount they receive is sufficient to provide for a basic, dignified living.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, on a brighter note, we can take comfort in the fact that for the same group of seniors 65 and above, 76% of them are property owners and the slew of Housing and Development Board (HDB) policies introduced in the recent years present many options open to these seniors who wish to unlock value in their homes, for a very comfortable retirement if they know how to do it.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, these housing monetisation options are not widely known and understood by seniors.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many seniors aged 65 and above received very little education and tend to leave financial matters in the hands of other family members.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They are ill-equipped to understand the options – too many and too complex – and, even if they do, I am always worried whether they can manage those money released judiciously.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: She approached me for financial assistance after her husband passed away.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Although we were able to secure some short-term assistance from the Government for Mdm Tan, she did not qualify for long-term financial assistance because of her son’s income as well as the option to monetise her flat.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: She found it a challenge every month to pay for her food, medical and utility bills, until we helped her realise the significant value of the asset she owns, that is, her 4-room flat.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: She is now often seen out and about in the community, happily enjoying the company of friends and hobbies like painting, visiting her doctor confidently and never having to worry about overdue bills.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But I am still concerned about Mdm Tan.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: She recently told me that her niece has suddenly become very friendly and has asked her that she be made a joint account holder of Mdm Tan’s now very healthy bank account.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Luckily, Mdm Tan listened to her Member of Parliament (MP) on the risks of doing so and she has held on tightly to her bank account, so far!

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, according to MOM, "triple weak" companies are those that do not meet the minimum criteria in terms of nurturing and having a Singaporean Core in their workforce and having a tangential reference to Singapore's economy and society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The prospects of Singaporeans being hired into such companies and doing well or getting promoted are low.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Does the Minister have an update on MOM's investigation into the remaining companies?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Separately, has there been a reduction in the prevalence of such "triple weak" companies?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What is the current number of companies that are under investigation and which industries do such companies predominate in?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How does the Ministry identify such companies and is there scope for greater enforcement, including whistleblowing channels, to identify such companies early?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What action does MOM take for companies that are uncooperative, show no improvement in their policies or slide back to their own ways of being "triple weak"?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister of Manpower mentioned at the last COS that some employers have the preconceived ideas that local PMETs are either unable or unwilling to work, so such companies write off Singaporeans without even considering them fairly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As there are practical limitations on MOM's ability to verify all certificates submitted, I would like to suggest MOM could advise employers to conduct verification via a panel of low-cost service providers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Verification need not be made a compulsory condition of granting the EP.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But there is every reason to believe that voluntary use of such a verification process would be high, should it be cheap and accessible.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After all, few employers would want to hire an employee who falsifies credentials.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Through this, we could cut down cases of such forgery of credentials.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is stated in press advisories that “MOM conducts proactive checks to detect and enforce against false applications.” However, this is a crime with a so-called “willing buyer and seller”, as both parties are incentivised to collude and conceal the facts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Right now, there is an MOM hotline for people to report infringements.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How many have used the hotline and how many successful prosecutions have resulted?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If effective, can we consider investing more resources to publicise this hotline?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And are there other means of proactive enforcement used?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, can more be done with artificial intelligence (AI) and data analytics to flag out suspicious activity for enforcement?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Mr Chairman, under the CPF Act, CPF members are allowed to transfer their savings to their parents and grandparents, provided the members satisfy certain conditions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: These provisions are useful to enable CPF members to help provide for the retirement needs of their family members, giving them some peace of mind and reducing intra-family poverty.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: These days, the formation of an immediate family nucleus should not be assumed to be the norm.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Many Singaporeans are single or childless in their senior years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: These persons will not have children or grandchildren who can top up their CPF balances.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: These are already relationships recognised under our law for inheritance of estates, and will help boost retirement adequacy of single and childless seniors.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: After that, we will probably have to confront ageism at work, health issues and rising cost of living.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The last thing we want to do at that point in time is to argue with the Government on when and how we can tap into our hard-earned CPF savings for retirement.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The question we should be asking ourselves is: by setting the auto payout at PEA, will it change the fundamental tenet of the CPF saving scheme in any way?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: There is not an iota of change at all.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Members can still choose to delay their payouts to earn more interest, if preferred.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Upon maturity date, you can expect to see your money deposited into your account with interest, unless you have instructed the bank to roll over the deposit.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I can assure the Minister that no members will quibble with the Government when they see their hard-earned money deposited into their accounts automatically on their PEA unless instructed otherwise.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The standard reply given was members must always strike a balance between retirement and housing needs.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some of these members were hauled to Court by the lenders, and each Court appearance would only push these members deeper into debt.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some of them were staring at a very real possibility of losing their flats.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: How is that amount even meaningful for retirement purposes?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: How long can these members stretch their payouts at PEA and how much would the payout be per month?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Can the CPF Board not feel the gravity of the predicament these members are facing?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It is not right to make these members beg to use their own money to save their flats.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: If there is no roof over a person's head, what is retirement?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: With his home intact, a member can still rent out a room or two to make ends meet.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The member can also explore the possibility of moving into a smaller flat when not under duress and use the proceeds for retirement.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: But all these options will vapourise if there is no flat left for the member to even plan his retirement.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Furthermore, any money used for property purchase would have to be returned to the member's CPF when the flat is sold with accrued interest.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: No one can siphon off any CPF money used for property purchase in any way.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The money is going straight back into the CPF and nowhere else.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: We certainly do not know when we will need to slow down or stop working completely before age 62.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: CPF members should be given the option and flexibility to plan their retirement needs at their own comfort level.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Let us decide if we are comfortable to take the lower payout at age 60 or wait out for a higher payout later.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Singaporeans have continued to support this Government despite knowing that they can no longer withdraw their money completely at age 55.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: They have continued to give this Government the mandate, knowing that they will not see their entire CPF savings until PEA and only in monthly payouts.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Why is this Government so reluctant to even offer such flexibility to Singaporeans in return?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: At times, we may have forgotten that there are people with disabilities that are left without a job.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This is even more critical for them as chances of learning a skill that can be used for future employment is as uncertain as them worrying about whether they have enough to care for themselves at old age.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This is a multifaceted issue that warrants more attention and support.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is understandable that we cannot cater jobs for the entire spectrum of special needs people.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But surely, there must be specific areas that we can champion together.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I recognise the awareness by employers that people with disabilities can also contribute economically has increased in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: General knowledge and broad skills may not help them to get more work opportunities as their curriculum is already different from those taught in the mainstream schools.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Once they are past the schooling age, there are even fewer institutions or higher learning avenues that can enable them to continue their skills upgrade or to learn the relevant knowledge that is in tandem with industry requirements.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With the growing gig economy and digital workplace, we can design and engage them in these areas.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We can consider providing platforms for them to further their studies and skills beyond their prescribed age where schools are currently able to keep them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Similar for those individuals with physical disabilities and are wheelchair bound, some are mentally well to cope with work and can be trained for suitable jobs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While some random efforts are taking place in Singapore, we should continue to learn from some companies, like Microsoft and CVS Health, that are proactive in employment practices in these areas.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I know that SG Enable actively supports people with disabilities in job training, employment information and job referrals to employers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: However, with an increasing number and a wider spectrum of people with special needs emerging due to awareness and medical advancement, we need to put in place earlier intervention to assist more special needs people in having an active income.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: I support these programmes that help make our workplaces and companies a lot more inclusive towards those who tend to be marginalised and who face challenges beyond just equal opportunities.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: How successful have these schemes been in hiring, training and integrating individuals with special needs or disabilities so as to help them to be financially independent and attain self-dignity?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: How can we build on efforts to help more individuals with special needs or disabilities to join the workforce?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Could MOM also provide more incentives to such employers to help them with job redesigns that can allow for FWAs so that individuals with special needs or disabilities can work from home or work from where it is convenient for them, and where they have more time and space to adjust to their new work environments and work responsibilities?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, working and holding a job is an important component of a good quality of life for everyone, regardless of abilities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Whether full- or part-time, work helps pay for one's daily living and also leads to better mental health and a sense of fulfilment and dignity.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In recent years, developments, such as the SG Enable unit, the Open Door Fund and SEC, have positively impacted the employment scene for persons with special needs or disabilities (PWDs).

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Employers, such as the United Overseas Bank, National Library Board, Starbucks, Uniqlo and others, have tapped on structured employment support services by voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs), such as the Movement for the Intellectually Disabled of Singapore (MINDS), the Society for the Physically Disabled (SPD) and the Autism Resource Centre (ARC).

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I have the following clarifications and recommendations for MOM's consideration.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What is the accountability of MOM to this special needs workforce?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How can it increase the employment rate of PWDs in Singapore?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How will MOM tap on its vast infrastructure and network to help them identify more suitable job families in both blue- and white-collar jobs?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Will MOM resource and support the hiring of inclusion managers to work with SG Enable and disability VWOs to customise skills frameworks for suitable job families identified?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Will MOM set targets to aspire major employers to up their hiring rate for PWDs?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, every worker, whether local or foreign, deserves to work in a safe environment.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Going forward, how can the adoption of technology help companies make further progress in workplace safety and health (WSH)?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can the Ministry share examples of companies that used technology to improve their WSH outcomes?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some businesses have also given feedback that after every fatal incident, additional safety measures are added.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While we all understand the importance of workplace safety, how can we also take into consideration legitimate business concerns about the associated cost of implementation as well its impact on productivity?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am not sure if it is true, but a resident told me that to change a light bulb, a company needs to have three workers – one to climb up the ladder, one to hold the ladder and a third who is a safety supervisor.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope this is not true, as risk must be measured against the cost of avoiding the risk.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Crossing the road also has risks but we understand intuitively that it does not make sense to have a safety supervisor at every zebra crossing.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope the Ministry can do a stocktake of the various WSH measures which have been implemented to see if any of these can be removed without compromising overall safety.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Yee, you might want to know that fall from height is a very common cause of serious injuries and fatalities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mr Chairman, I touched on WSH in my Budget Debate speech and spoke about the need to continually invest in our WSH practices to ensure that our workers can return home safely to their families every day.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I mentioned four areas that we could do more to safeguard our workers' safety and health.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, I called for our tripartite partners to place more emphasis on workplace health.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will cause a gradual shift in the types of WSH issues we will see in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, we will likely see more cases of chronic occupational diseases.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Poor workplace health contributes to work-related injuries and fatalities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to place a greater emphasis on workplace health sooner, rather than later, to address such issues early.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Either we were extremely lucky that the accidents did not lead to a fatality, or that today's better medical science has saved victims of serious accidents from possible death.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Whatever the reason may be, we need to do more to encourage companies to reduce the number of accidents at our workplaces.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Having a tiered insurance framework where companies will have to pay higher insurance premiums if there are many claims of the same incident nature will go some way towards achieving this.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Making WSH more pervasive in every industry will be no easy feat, especially if you consider the diverse nature of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Every industry has its own unique balance of local to foreign workforce ratio, and the nationalities within the foreign workforce are diverse.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The fact that we have too many training vendors that conduct the WSH Workforce Skills Qualification (WSG) courses – about a dozen at my last count – and the significant variance in training resources provided by these vendors, make implementing a standardised culture of WSH even more challenging.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A centralised WSH Academy can also serve as a Centre of Excellence in WSH.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Centre can establish a central registry of WSH practitioners, share industry best practices and showcase the use of new technologies to strengthen safety standards.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our SMEs would be the biggest beneficiaries from such a Centre of Excellence, as they have limited resources and will not be able to invest heavily in developing new WSH technologies.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: All workers deserve to go home safe and in good health to their families and loved ones every day.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Labour Movement stands ready to work with our tripartite partners on suggestions and proposals to raise WSH standards across Singapore so that we can all benefit from safer and healthier workplaces.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Chairman, there are many workers who are owed salaries due to company closure, and many are not able to recover their salaries.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They decided against Writ of Sale and Seizure (WSS) due to the high cost of filing for WSS relative to the amount of salary owed.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There is still a claim limit since the intention is to help workers tide over while looking for alternative employment.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In Singapore, we do not have an NIF.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Mr Chairman, the announcement that the Foreign Worker Quota for the services sector would be reduced has once again put a spotlight on migrant workers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: While the Dependency Ratio Ceilings for the other sectors remain unchanged for now, it is important that we continually take steps to focus on improving productivity at our workplaces.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: With selected training, these migrant workers can contribute to productivity improvements.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Having safe and conducive employment conditions is important to ensure that Singapore remains a choice employment destination for our migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: As part of the Work Permit application process, we need to better educate employers on their responsibilities to the migrant workers they employ.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Having a common understanding on the rights of migrant workers will serve to prevent potential disputes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Today, distressed migrant workers are unwilling to come forward when they have disputes against their employers, for fear of repatriation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: While MOM has made key changes to the employment transfer system for Work Permit holders to specifically address this, migrant workers often do not have the correct network or assistance to search for new jobs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: To exacerbate matters, workers who have lodged complaints are seen in a negative light by recruiters.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Employers, too, need to recognise that employing such workers can be advantageous, as these migrant workers have already acclimatised to local culture and work habits.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Regulating foreign employment agents (EAs) remains a challenge.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Has the Ministry considered giving unemployed foreign workers who are already in Singapore an advantage for re-employment?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Further, does the Ministry plan to take more resolute action against employers taking kickbacks from workers, whether transacted in Singapore or abroad?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: A recent 2018 Institute of Mental Health (IMH) study showed that one in seven Singaporeans experience a mental health condition in their lifetime.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: This means that an increasing segment of our workforce will have to grapple with mental health conditions while under employment.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Yet, studies have shown that an overwhelming 86.5% of those employed do not seek help for their mental health difficulties.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Members have now heard me share the above in this House that MOM’s intent to recognise and promote employee well-being can be further served by enacting clear and deliberate provisions that are upstream and preventive in nature.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: First, that the definition of "well-being" in all statutes, regulations and policies pertaining to employment in Singapore must expressly include not only physical but also psychosocial well-being.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Accordingly, the relevant provisions in the WSH Act, as well as subsidiary legislation, must provide for the psychosocial health and safety of employees at the workplace.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Second, workplace well-being begins with destigmatising mental health conditions and conversations.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: In positive language, this means that we must foster inclusive employment practices.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Such measures include prohibiting discriminatory employment practices, such as compulsory declaration of medical history, especially for mental health conditions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: That is, of course, until such information no longer prejudices a potential candidate.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Ultimately, we are aiming for an employment climate that does not harbour misconceptions and prejudgments about applicants with mental health experiences.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Each group is vulnerable to different work conditions connected to greater psychological hazards which include discrimination, higher risk of physical injury and challenges in social integration.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Will the Ministry allocate budget and manpower to look into the increased mental health risks present in such segments of our job market?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The majority of those which did not were planning to do so.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It has been five years since the last survey.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: To get a more accurate picture of the situation, the survey should include interviews of employees and job applicants and not just employers, as the then Minister of State Teo Ser Luck said, would be the case for the next survey in employment exchange in 2016.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: TAFEP sets an important framework for protecting workers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: According to the Government's Report in December 2018, "there are enforcement mechanisms that complement these guidelines.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For instance, if employers are found to have discriminatory hiring practices, such as posting discriminatory job advertisements, MOM restricts such employers' ability to hire foreign workers in Singapore".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: MOM can consider ensuring Government agencies and Ministries avoid procuring services and goods from companies placed on the FCF watchlist.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Economic incentives can also be given to companies which consistently do well and are not on the watchlist as a means of encouraging fair employment practices.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Mr Chairman, it is not uncommon to find restraint of trade clauses in employment contracts to protect the interest of the employer, by restricting a former employee from competing in the same industry and jumping to a competitor.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Such restrictions are currently not governed by legislation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: As a result, we hear of instances of unreasonable restraint clauses built into contracts even for workers, such as cleaners, construction workers, preschool teachers and even drivers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: It often states that the employee cannot work in the same or similar industry for one year after leaving the employment of the company.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Such unreasonable restriction of trade clauses jeopardises the livelihoods of our workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: I urge the Ministry to introduce measures to protect the interest of vulnerable segments of our workers, including low-wage workers and junior PMEs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 2.53 pm until 3.20 pm.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, I declare my interest as a Professor in the Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD) and as a founding committee member of the Singapore Computer Society's Women in Technologies, Special Interest Group.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I greatly appreciate the various provisions that have been announced in this year's Budget to better recognise the needs and contributions of women.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, there are distinct benefits to greater gender diversity across all industries but perhaps especially so in the technology sector.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In Caroline Perez's book "Invisible Women", exposing data bias in a world designed for men, she provides compelling evidence to show how the silencing of women's needs and perspectives can be costly and downright fatal: crash test dummies that are based on the average male physique, ill-fitting armour that fails to protect policewomen, and cancer research based principally on data on the male immune system.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: These are all sobering examples of how the omission of women's needs can cost lives.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: As our society is technologising rapidly, the digital and physical infrastructures that shape much of our everyday lives must necessarily reflect the needs of all and not just half of humanity.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: We must thus ensure that the distinct strengths of women and our valuable insights are given every opportunity to shape technology and design.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: After all, research shows that women have tremendous socio-emotional intelligence.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: We are logical and rational thinkers and also possess the self-awareness, perception and social skills that are crucial for understanding people, interpreting difficult situations and resolving conflicting needs.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Women also continue to bear most of the responsibilities as caregivers, caring not just for the next generation, but also for the elderly in our ageing society.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Women's perspectives are thus especially illuminating for improving the innovations and services that facilitate the performance of such critical duties.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: To say it is difficult for women to balance the needs of home with the pressures of career is, therefore, a gross understatement.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In a fast-moving sector, such as technology, the task of reintegrating is significantly more daunting as one's skills become quickly outdated.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Because there are fewer women to rise to the top, younger women do not see sufficient female role models in the technology sector.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: They are thus discouraged from joining the sector or they leave prematurely, uncertain of their future prospects.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Upstream as well, we must try our best to boost the number of women in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) so that we can nurture the next generation of women technological leaders.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, our female students bring well-rounded perspectives and refreshing ideas when working in collaboration with their male counterparts.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: As professors, we can easily tell which projects have female team members because their innovations and designs invariably have that special touch.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: So, what initiatives can we introduce to increase gender diversity in male-dominated sectors?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: However, we also need to better support women who take leave for pregnancy, childcare or eldercare to help them sustain and broaden their professional networks.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: This will help smoothen their path as they return to the workforce.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Can we, therefore, introduce credit programmes that can help defray the cost of membership in professional societies?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Can we also have special incentives for companies in sectors where women are under-represented, to introduce more FWAs and better childcare support?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: And can we also foster more incubation schemes that cater to the circumstances of female innovators and that offer more systematic mentoring?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Mr Chairman, FWAs, when implemented effectively, can save businesses money, reduce operating costs and boost productivity and bringing advantages across the economy for both businesses as well as the entire supply chain.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Benefits include business and individual productivity, lower cost for workspace for companies, and many hours saved from travelling to and from the workplace.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: With the competitive labour market, FWAs may be a staff attraction and retention tool for businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: We are witnessing the evolution of work arrangements changing beyond just FWAs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The gig economy and the increasing number of startups are changing the corporate workplace and how we work.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: We are also seeing new models of industry spaces, for example, with JTC LaunchPad, dedicated or shared co-working spaces offered by players like WeWorks, CollectiveWorks, The Great Room, just to name a few.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Technology, like mobile computing, high bandwidth and connectivity, data analytics, automation, robotics and AI, are shaping how we work and where we work.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: This is impacting both large and small businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: We are seeing a trend of work arrangements becoming more casual, less structured and less centrally controlled.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: With technological advancements and disruptions, many organisations are seeing flexible workspaces and arrangements as strategic tools to drive change and to get their employees to innovate.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: So, it is no longer a matter of just providing FWAs to meet employee needs and demands or FWAs just for work-life balance that employees are demanding but, together with the redesign of work and workspaces, FWAs are becoming strategic tools for businesses to innovate, improve productivity, attract and retain talent.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Co-working spaces also provide for the advantage of ecosystems of support, collaboration and sharing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: So, against this backdrop, people will require new skills and knowledge to work.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The new skills required in this new landscape of work include critical thinking and problem-solving, ability to deal with and make sense of data/information, ability to collaborate and influence others, effective communication skills, adaptability, learning and relearning skills, being self-directed and creative.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: How are we preparing our workers to thrive in this new world of work?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: To encourage more companies to accept and employ persons with special needs, we have to help them understand that there are many types of special needs, physical and mental, and the kind of jobs these different groups can do.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Public education and greater support from the Government are very important in this regard.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Perhaps the Government would also consider setting annual employment targets to employ persons with special needs in the public sector.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Employers have to take the plunge, start hiring and learn along the way how they could be more supportive and understanding.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Fellow workers will also benefit as they learn more about empathy.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: It is important that we help persons with special needs achieve as much independence as possible through work.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Employment enables them to be engaged in society, learn and make meaningful contributions, just like able-bodied persons.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: They can help relieve their families' burdens and their parents can take comfort in the knowledge that they will be able to cope even after their parents are no longer around.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: The other group of Singaporeans whom we should make greater effort to integrate into our workplace are ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Employment plays an important role in keeping recidivism rates down.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: When ex-offenders receive the chance to be contributing and be valuable members of society again, they can regain their personal dignity and make a living to support themselves and their families.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Persuading companies to consider ex-offenders has its own set of challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Members for all of your cuts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, I am always mindful that there are residents who would like to work but have not found jobs, and there are also those whose jobs and wages have not improved.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MOM will try our best to help everyone.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, the global economic environment is more uncertain.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As a result, MTI has moderated our growth forecast.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The employment rate for seniors has risen steadily over the years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The unemployment rate among seniors is also quite low, actually lower than average.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Still, not all seniors who want to, have jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They are not keeping up with the rest of our economy and their peers in other developed countries.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the medium to longer term, what are the prospects to improve job quality and grow wages in these sectors?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: That is why we are moderating foreign manpower growth in Services.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But we have to spur further efforts to restructure.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members of Parliament have given their view on this move during the Budget Debate and MTI's COS debate.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But first, I will provide an overview of MOM's responses to all Members' cuts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
