text: As a society, it is also important to care for our workers' well-being, especially vulnerable workers, such as our lower-income workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In addition to enhancing our lower-income workers' wages and employability, I agree with Mr Zainal Sapari and Dr Intan Mokhtar that care should be extended to their working conditions and how they are treated at work.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Take, for example, access to proper rest areas which Dr Intan Mokhtar raised.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Workers need a safe and conducive environment for their rest breaks, such as their meals.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Yet, we have encountered cases of cleaners having to use makeshift rest areas at stairwells and in open public areas.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Such situations can be improved and, going forward, MOM will look into companies’ practices in giving workers access to proper rest areas.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is a place where cleaners can take breaks, have meals and safekeep their belongings.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I strongly encourage all service buyers and employers to do the same.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Fellow Singaporeans, we need to do our part, too, and treat our lower-income workers with dignity and respect.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Some of the simple and practical ways to uplift them include returning our own trays at the hawker centres, thanking them for their work and giving them time to rest during their breaks.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Ultimately, society must view our lower-income workers also as persons of worth and deserving of our respect.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Zainal Sapari also asked MOM to review whether a scheme could provide financial or subsistence relief to help rank-and-file workers who are owed salaries due to company closure.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: If employers fail to do so because the company has closed down, employees can commence debt recovery by applying to the State Courts for a Writ of Seizure and Sale (WSS).

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: MOM will assist lower-income claimants through the WSS process, including providing financial aid.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management (TADM) will also refer them to MSF and their Social Service Offices for assistance on ComCare if needed.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Similarly, the same way we protect our lower-income workers, we should also safeguard the well-being of our foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: They share a common purpose in contributing to our society, through building our homes and schools, working in our hospitals and factories, and keeping our environment clean.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As we moderate the intake of foreign workers, treating them with respect can help us retain skilled and experienced workers, as some Members have asked for.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Ms Anthea Ong suggested to extend MOM's regulatory reach to overseas employment agencies.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: She also asked if MOM could take a more resolute action against employers taking kickbacks from workers, whether transacted in Singapore or overseas.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Within Singapore, MOM prohibits employment agencies in Singapore from charging workers beyond the stipulated fee cap.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: However, we do not have the jurisdiction to act against agents taking kickbacks in other countries.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is not a matter that we have a choice over.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This includes foreign employment agencies that tie-up with local agents, or the overseas operations of local employment agencies.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Nonetheless, we will do what we can here.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Since 2012, employers are prohibited from collecting kickbacks from foreign workers in consideration for employment.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And Mr Leon Perera asked about MOM's hotline.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We received 102 calls last year, of which we followed up and investigated 49 calls.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The rest were just enquiries and there was no follow-up required.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But one thing I want to assure Members is that let us know, and we will investigate each of these cases seriously if there are credible leads.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Additionally, whenever our investigations reveal suspicious or irregular practices by overseas agents, information is shared with our foreign embassies to enlist their help to combat any malpractices in their respective countries.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As Mr Melvin Yong rightfully pointed out, we need to educate employers on their obligations to foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For example, MOM regularly updates the work pass obligations of employers in the employers’ copy of the In-principle Approval letter.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Employers are also kept informed of new and existing work pass requirements through direct mailers and on MOM’s website.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Ms Anthea Ong and Mr Melvin Yong suggested that we improve the employment system to retain skilled and experienced foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Given the constraints on the number of foreign workers we can bring in, we want to ensure that each worker we bring in counts and their skills and experience can be retained in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, this reinforces the capability, productivity and safety.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For instance, more experienced construction workers were less likely to suffer work injuries.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: MOM has supported the recruitment and retention of experienced foreign workers in the following ways.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Traditional Source and North Asian Source Work Permit holders are not subject to a maximum period of employment.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For Non-Traditional Source and People's Republic of China (PRC) Work Permit holders, MOM has, over the years, extended the maximum period of employment to encourage companies to retain their trained and experienced workers, to raise overall workforce productivity.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In response to industry feedback, MOM last increased the maximum period of employment by four years in all sectors in 2018.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For foreign workers in the Construction and Process sectors, they can be transferred to another employer, upon the agreement of their existing employers, or the expiry of their Work Permits.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: They are given about a month to look for new employers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We also allow all foreign workers to find another employer if they have valid claims.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: While they are given two weeks to seek new employment, we have given short extensions on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Melvin Yong hoped to see greater assistance for foreign workers involved in disputes with their employers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The majority of these foreign workers came from the Construction sector, about nine in 10.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To improve their job facilitation outcomes, the Singapore Contractors Association Ltd (SCAL) has made available the Foreign Construction Worker Directory System (FCWDS) that facilitates their search for new employers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As a society, we must, therefore, strive to make work conditions safer and healthier for our workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Singapore has made good progress in our WSH performance.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Yee Chia Hsing asked how our progress compares to other developed countries.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Such progress was made possible by a major shift in WSH culture, mindset and practices, enabled by strong tripartism.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The WSH Council, comprising employer and union representatives, worked closely with Trade Associations and Chambers (TACs) to tackle the leading causes of workplace fatalities.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This included the "Target Zero Falls" campaign, where SCAL encouraged industry partners to conduct senior management walkabouts for work-at-heights activities.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For MOM, we continued to maintain a strong enforcement presence, especially in higher-risk industries.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But we must do better, so that our workers can return home safe and healthy.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is an ambitious goal, but an achievable one.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Only four countries amongst the OECD countries have achieved it so far.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We must also keep an eye on non-fatal injuries.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Compared to 2017, we saw a 3% rise in numbers in 2018.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: One in three working residents have either diabetes, high blood pressure or high cholesterol, which can affect safety as well if the condition is not managed well.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We agree with Mr Melvin Yong that a greater emphasis on workplace health is, indeed, necessary to address its potential impact on safety.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I see three main ways to improve further.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: First, we need company management to be committed to improving WSH within their companies.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Top management, including at the Board level, is best-placed to influence the company’s WSH culture, as they control its resources, policies and practices.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: A good example is Lendlease, an international property and infrastructure company with operations here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: A Board member chairs its Sustainability Committee that is responsible for setting the WSH policy and strategic directions for Lendlease.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In addition, WSH performance is discussed at all Board meetings, with the CEO and top management all held accountable.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In the fourth image, Members can see Lendlease's Paya Lebar Quarter project.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is one example where the leadership has taken ownership to champion progressive WSH practices, such as a near-miss reporting regime, WSH data analytics, as well as Building Information Modelling (BIM) techniques.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: With WSH as a top business priority, Lendlease's strong WSH track record has served as a competitive advantage in helping them to win repeat business.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, they see WSH as a competitive advantage against competitors.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Second, we need greater emphasis on workplace health.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To address the potential impact of poorly managed health on workplace safety, the WSH Council partnered Health Promotion Board (HPB) to introduce Total WSH.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Total WSH involves injury and occupational disease prevention, together with occupational health promotion, through health screening, physical activities, healthier diet initiatives, and adjustments in work processes, so that those with chronic conditions can continue to work safely.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We agree with Mr Melvin Yong that more can be done, and we encourage the Labour Movement to partner us to encourage more companies to adopt Total WSH.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Third, WSH is another aspect where we can win with technology.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Companies can leverage technology advancements, such as sensors, predictive analytics and the Internet of Things to more effectively manage WSH risks.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Woodlands Transport and SIA Engineering Company have taken part in MOM's WSH Tech Challenge to testbed a fatigue detection and management device among their vehicle drivers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As Members can see in the fifth image, this device uses sensors and image processing technology to track the micro-movements of a driver’s head, eyes and facial expressions to detect fatigue.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Those who show signs of fatigue will be alerted by an alarm from a buzzer and seat vibration, and 93% fewer fatigue episodes were detected among drivers whose vehicles were equipped with the device, when compared to the baseline.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Melvin Yong also spoke about leveraging technology to make WSH training more productive and realistic and I agree.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I recently tried virtual reality training that simulates working at heights.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As Members can see in the sixth image, I experienced a virtual fall from a height of 14 storeys.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I can tell you it is quite realistic.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: You stand on the ledge and then fall off.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This ingrained the importance of following safety procedures as they could make a difference between life and death.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Melvin Yong suggested forming a National Training Academy that consolidates training resources and ensures high and consistent WSH standards.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: SkillsFuture Singapore has set a consistent standard for WSQ training providers in terms of curriculum and training methods.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But we will consider how to improve training further and will study this idea further with our tripartite partners.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Yee Chia Hsing shared businesses’ concern that MOM would introduce safety requirements after every fatal accident.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: He used the example of three workers having to change a light bulb to highlight the need to balance requirements.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Some Members may know the riddle, "How many people do you need to screw a light bulb?" But then, the light bulb flashed and I suddenly got a certain insight.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: If you look at the other end of the scale, Mr Melvin Yong also asked to introduce more WSH requirements for better worker protection.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, there is this balance that you have to manage between protecting workers and what businesses consider as too many requirements.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The contrasting views by both Members show the tension between having more regulations that could be overly prescriptive versus being too lax such that WSH is compromised.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is why we have adopted a balanced approach under the WSH Act's outcome-based regime.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Companies and individuals are responsible for taking reasonably practicable measures to ensure workers' safety and health.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This gives stakeholders the flexibility to adopt cost-effective WSH measures.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: There is no need for a worker to hold a ladder if it is securely fixed and stable, such as a platform ladder with guardrails.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: If the ladder is not securely fixed, I suggest have someone hold it, because, as Speaker mentioned earlier, it is also for safety.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: There is also no need for the supervisor to be present all the time if the workers have been informed earlier on safety measures.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Therefore, with the right equipment, the ladder is not costly, and with the right measures, only one worker is needed to change the light bulb.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We welcome employers who need advice to consult MOM and the WSH Council.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Better results can often be achieved through strengthening WSH ownership within company management.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Uncommitted companies may hire a trained WSH representative to meet the letter of the law, but not follow through with internal systems to support the WSH representative in identifying and preventing hazards.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Only with ownership, would companies be self-motivated to adopt WSH practices without us prescribing more requirements.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Chairman, allow me to recap the enhancements to the Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) scheme in Malay.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: (In Malay):  	To ensure that lower-income workers can progress together with the other workers, we have improved their lives through the WIS scheme that tops up their salaries and helps them save for retirement.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Most WIS recipients also receive other forms of Government support to help meet their living needs, for example, Mr Gunasegaran, a 49-year-old cleaning supervisor.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: He lives in a three-room flat with his wife and three children.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Apart from WIS, he also receives Goods and Services Tax (GST) Vouchers and U-Save rebates to help offset his daily household expenses.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: His two daughters receive financial assistance from MOE and receive free textbooks and school attire and public transport credit.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: His youngest son in preschool receives the Kindergarten Financial Assistance and Mr Guna only needs to pay about $1 monthly.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Our approach of providing multi-layered support is more responsive to the varied needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Let us further strengthen these successful efforts and continue to work hard to improve the lives of Singapore workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: (In English): In conclusion, the Government is committed to fostering an inclusive and caring society.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To this end, we will continue to integrate persons with special needs into the workforce, improve the well-being of lower-income workers, safeguard the well-being of foreign workers, and make work conditions safer and healthier for all workers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Chairman, Minister Josephine Teo and Minister of State Zaqy Mohamad spoke about our efforts to provide better support and assurance for our workers, and how we can walk the tech journey together.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As we strive to improve our workers' skills, wages and employability, workplaces should also be progressive and inclusive, so that each segment of the workforce is valued and can realise their potential.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As NTUC Deputy Secretary-General Heng Chee How mentioned in his Budget speech, "Every Worker Matters to the overall good of our economy, our society and our country." We agree.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We will press on with our efforts to help young graduates get off to a good start in their careers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We will continue to support women so that they can fulfil both career and family aspirations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We will also do more to help ex-offenders find meaningful employment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Young Singaporeans are the future of our nation, and we want to maximise the opportunities for them to take up meaningful jobs and careers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: However, some may need more help in improving their job search skills to find suitable employment, as for most young people, it is their first time applying for a job.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked how graduating students can benefit from the Career Starter Programme, which I first announced last year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The Career Starter Programme, which is part of WSG's A&G initiative, is supported by ITE and polytechnics.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This is a resource pack that equips graduating students with useful information for their job search.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Within the pack are useful tips and advice on what graduates should consider when applying for a job, where to find work opportunities, how to ace job interviews, and how to manage their money when they start work, disseminated to 28,000 graduates this year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Second, there are interactive Career Booster workshops to improve our young graduates’ job search strategies and skills.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: These workshops are designed to provide more hands-on help, such as good resume writing techniques, and approaches to the job search that can uncover different career opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Third, the Career Starter Programme offers personalised career coaching and other tailored support for graduating students who may require more in-depth assistance provided by career coaches from WSG's Careers Connect.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: I now move on to our efforts to equip and reintegrate ex-offenders.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The labour market is changing rapidly, with technology advancing and industries transforming.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Those who have been out of the workforce for a significant period of time, like ex-offenders, are concerned about gaining relevant skills and reintegrating into society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Chong Kee Hiong asked how we are supporting ex-offenders in employment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: I am pleased to inform them that WSG works closely with SCORE to help ex-offenders find gainful employment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Research conducted by the Singapore Prison Service has shown that when ex-offenders are meaningfully engaged in their jobs, it eases their reintegration into the community which, in turn, helps to lower recidivism.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: To arm ex-offenders with skills and improve their chances in employment, we have two programmes under the A&G initiative, namely, Project Phoenix and Career Trial.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Since 2007, Project Phoenix has been providing training and employment assistance to ex-offenders to prepare them for reintegration into the workforce.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We hope that more employers will step forward to offer job opportunities to ex-offenders who can prove to be valuable workers when given a second chance.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The tight labour market and slowing workforce growth also present compelling reasons for employers to tap on every available worker.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Chairman, as we look to better support young graduates and ex-offenders, we are also committed to making our workplaces more progressive and inclusive for women.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Today, we have a healthy employment situation for women in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: But our proportion of women in part-time employment is still below OECD average.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We recognise that there is still much that we can do to better support women at workplaces.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: MOM’s A&G initiative offers a suite of job matching services and other programmes to help jobseekers, including women who wish to return to the workforce.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As Minister Josephine has announced, the Career Trial scheme will be enhanced to include part-time jobs as well, and this will expand the opportunities for those who are only able to work part-time.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We understand that most women juggle multiple roles, including the women Parliamentarians in this Chamber, at home and at work and also our own aspirations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: I completely agree with Prof Lim Sun Sun and Deputy Secretary-General Heng Chee How that women need not be forced to choose between career and family.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Career and family really need not be binary options.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Instead, with the right workplace support, women can fulfil our career aspirations while meeting our family responsibilities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This was the key thrust of my speech in this Chamber at the recent Parliamentary Motions on Ageing with Purpose and Support for Caregivers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Back then, I spoke about the Government’s resolve to develop a workplace culture that is supportive of FWAs and the promotion of greater adoption of FWAs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Chong Kee Hiong will be pleased to know that, compared to five years ago, more workplaces in Singapore are offering FWAs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: It either means unplanned time-off or ad hoc teleworking.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The trend of higher FWA adoption across the board is not only good news for employees; it is also positive for companies.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Among workplace practices, the provision of FWA has the greatest impact on staff retention which benefit companies with experienced and engaged workers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We want to keep the momentum of FWA adoption going.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This will allow more companies to benefit from the grant to sustain their employees’ FWA adoption, including job-sharing by PMETs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The guide aims to raise awareness on job sharing and educate employers on the nuts and bolts of implementing such a scheme.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Job sharing would not only expand the range of FWA options.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: It can enhance trust, commitment and work satisfaction between employees and employers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We are optimistic that more employers are recognising the value FWAs bring.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Since the Tripartite Standard on FWAs was launched in October 2017, responses have grown.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Key adopters of the Tripartite Standards include those in the public sector.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Our Public Service agencies are committed to creating a conducive work environment that allows officers to achieve good work and personal goals.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This includes providing public officers with suitable FWA options.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Take, for example, the Accountant-General's Department (AGD) in the Ministry of Finance.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Two of its employees, Ms Lim Yu May and Ms Emily Kao were given a job-sharing arrangement in cash management and payment processing.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This suited the two mothers well as they appreciated the newfound flexibility to look after their family needs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Yu May took the morning shift so she could be home for two primary school children.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Emily, on the other hand, preferred to work in the afternoons while her toddler took his afternoon nap under her mother's watch.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: To ensure a smooth handover, Yu May and Emily would spend their overlapping hour at noon to exchange information and discuss what needed to be followed up.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: They kept abreast of each other’s progress via an excel spreadsheet that was constantly updated.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Their successful job-sharing arrangement lasted for about one-and-a-half years from December 2013 to June 2015.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: When Emily had her second child, she was granted extended maternity leave.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Yu May took no pay leave for one-and-a-half years to care for her children.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: They have kept pace with their careers and training opportunities that the organisation offers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We hope more employers will step up their FWAs and gain from the experience and loyalty of committed staff.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: To spread the adoption of FWAs, we will work closely with our tripartite partners to reach out to trade associations, businesses, chambers and employers about the Work-Life Grant and the Tripartite Standard on FWAs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Encouraging more FWAs will also support the employment of older workers, which the Minister for Manpower, Ms Josephine Teo, spoke about earlier.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As our seniors age, there will be a growing need for greater flexibility in workplaces so as to meet their diverse needs and preferences.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Many of them may wish to remain in the workforce, but with reduced or differing work intensity.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As we move towards a more inclusive work culture and mindset, we will be better placed to make the best of our talents.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: With family-friendly workplaces, employees can contribute their fullest potential without compromising their responsibilities to their loved ones.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: And age-friendly work practices let our seniors pass on valuable experience and knowledge as they work at their preferred pace and intensity.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: At this juncture, could I seek Mr Chairman's permission to spend a few more minutes to completely respond to the cuts of the Members?

speaker: The Chairman
text: As we are running a bit ahead of schedule, I will give you a few more minutes, provided you do not speak in more than four languages.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Chairman, as we try to harness the full capabilities of our workforce, I agree with Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Desmond Choo that workplace harassment is an area that deserves greater attention.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: A safe workplace allows employees to work optimally.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: For that to take place, both employers and employees must have an interest and responsibility in preventing and managing workplace harassment.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: There are two broad categories of workplace harassment and they are dealt with differently.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This kind of harassment will be addressed by the Courts or the Police and an affected employee may also seek civil remedies directly through the Courts, such as a Protection Order, against the harasser.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Now, for cases that may not come under POHA, we want to ensure that companies have a robust grievance handling process to deal with such claims of workplace harassment.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We also encourage companies to take clear steps to prevent and manage workplace harassment.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: These include: (a) being explicit about what is considered unacceptable behaviour at the workplace; (b) making clear the disciplinary actions that would be taken against perpetrators of workplace harassment; (c) having in place safe avenues for affected employees to surface their complaints to management for recourse; and (d) providing adequate support for affected employees, for example, giving them time off or the flexibility to work from home during the investigation and/or recovery.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: First, TAFEP seeks to help companies put in place robust processes to manage workplace harassment complaints.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Second, TAFEP will also be an avenue for employees who face workplace harassment to seek advice and assistance.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Affected employees can call 6838 0969, or approach TAFEP or write to TAFEP.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Should they wish to share their case in confidence, TAFEP will certainly respect their request and not alert their employers.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: TAFEP is also working with relevant Government agencies and partners, including the Police, the Courts, and the Association of Women for Action and Research (AWARE) to set up a referral process so that TAFEP can have sight of all workplace harassment cases.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We will take a whole-of-Government approach to support affected employees.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: As pointed out by Mr Desmond Choo, some affected employees may need counselling services.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: TAFEP will help advise employers on where to obtain such support services and put them in touch with relevant agencies.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Companies that put in place programmes, such as peer support or counselling, will help their staff cope better with the stress and effects of harassment.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Chairman, preventing and addressing discriminatory and unfair employment practices are key to making workplaces more inclusive and progressive.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I wish to assure Ms Anthea Ong, Mr Faisal Manap and Mr Melvin Yong that MOM takes a serious view of any form of workplace discrimination or unfair employment practices.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Employers should abide by the Tripartite Guidelines on Fair Employment Practices, which set out principles for fair and merit-based employment practices.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Even as we constantly reach out to employers to educate them about the Guidelines, I want to ensure Members that we will and have taken actions against employers who are found to have engaged in discriminatory employment practices.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I would also like to assure Mr Melvin Yong that there have been instances where we have asked employers to remove or refrain from enforcing unreasonable contractual terms.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We want employees to know that there is help available for those with unreasonable clauses in their employment contracts or are unfairly discriminated against.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: They can approach their unions, TAFEP or MOM for assistance.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Chairman, please allow me to take one minute to just say a few words in Mandarin.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: (In Mandarin):  	Today, the global competition for talents is stiff and technology is developing rapidly.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: For our workers to be future-ready, MOM is committed to uplift our workers' skills and employability and will ensure that our employment practices are fair, inclusive and progressive.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: On the one hand, it will help all workers, including young graduates, women, older workers and ex-offenders find suitable employment.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: On the other hand, it will help companies’ grow competitively and tap on a wider pool of capabilities.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: For many years, MOM has been promoting FWAs so that employees can fulfil both career and non-work responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: (In English): Chairman, for a nation with no natural resources, every Singaporean is an important asset.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: With increasing competition for scarce talent, having progressive and inclusive workplaces will enable companies to tap on a wider pool of capabilities.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: To do so, we need a whole-of-society effort where workers, young and old, employers from all sectors and the community at large to play their part.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Only then can we realise our collective potential together as a nation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Chairman, there is a point of clarification for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Earlier in my cut, I mentioned about PME union representation, in particular, the review of section 17(3) of the Industrial Relations Act as well as the review of the Tripartite Guidelines.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I wanted a response from the Minister whether the tripartite partners can look into this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Chairman, I thank the Minister for the response.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I wish to make a clarification, and I have two clarifications to seek.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The clarification I want to make is this: I do believe in the statutory protections to protect the workers from being summarily dismissed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: But I think that the protection should be delinked from their retirement and have no age limit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: But I guess that is an argument for another time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: So, I am going to seek two clarifications based on the Minister's response.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The first clarification is on the statutory protection, specifically on termination with notice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Valid reasons for termination are misconduct, poor performance and redundancy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: So, I want to confirm that employees terminated with notice can go to MOM to file a complaint for invalid dismissal and MOM will help to reinstate the employee.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: My concern is that employees might think that termination with notice is valid dismissal just because notice period is given and, therefore, this becomes some kind of loophole and makes the current statutory protections until retirement age meaningless, as employers can then prematurely retire employees using the termination-with-notice clause.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The second clarification is the last time the re-employment age was raised to 67, the then Minister of Manpower, Mr Lim Swee Say, said that the tripartite partners hit a wall on raising the retirement age because employers objected to the further increase in business impact on the bottom line.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: And, more importantly, younger workers objected because they do not want their career progression to be stalled.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: So, without revealing the number of years you are going to increase for re-employment age, how have the workgroup members overcome this particular objection, especially from the younger workers, in terms of career progression?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: How did the workgroup overcome the concerns of the younger workers?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Member is right in pointing out that the younger workers did have a concern about whether there would be impediments to their own progression.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But what eventually was able to swing the thinking of all the workers is that all of us will get there.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The younger workers today will eventually, at some point in time, not be so young.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And they would like the enhancements to apply to themselves, too.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But there is still a very important consideration, which is, that in terms of how employers and businesses are going to manage their workforce, they are going to need flexibility in moving people around, meaning that employers are quite conscious of the importance of freeing up certain positions so that the younger ones have a chance to gain the experience and also have the opportunity to progress in their career.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That is why it is still very important to give employers certain flexibility in managing their workforce and not try to impose too many rules on them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: On the Member's first question, I am a little bit puzzled why the Member would consider that when a notice period is required and, indeed, forms part of the termination, then it is considered meaningless protection.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As to whether the outcome of the investigation and as to whether it will order a reinstatement, in most cases, the worker does not want reinstatement either, because the relationship has soured and they would rather move on.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Chairman, I have two clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: First, is there any plan to rebrand the Services sector to make it more sexy and more attractive to local workers, especially the younger workers?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The second clarification is: will the Minister reconsider my suggestion of letting SMEs, especially the smaller SMEs, to retain their S Pass holders so that they do not need to send back their workers who are already well-trained and know the job well and, hence, affect their operations?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And this is not just for Nee Soon South.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is also for Bishan Toa Payoh Group Representation Constituency (GRC) and Hong Kah GRC and the rest of Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I was afraid the Member was going to say Batam and Johor, too!

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: All the sector agencies that are involved in any of the services sector industry transformation, in fact, have it very much as a priority.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They are aware that, with this tightening, there would be some firms that will be affected and they would want to take advantage of this opportunity, not just to rebrand.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If the substance of it has not changed, I do not think job seekers are unable to tell the difference.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ultimately, everyone wants to progress in their careers, and we should try our very best to ensure that, whichever sector they are in, they do have the opportunity to advance.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, I rise to reply to the question that was asked by the Minister for Manpower.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A similar question, I believe, was asked by Minister of State Zaqy Mohamad during the Budget Debate and I rose at the end of that debate to say that the Workers' Party supports the Budget but subject to our opposition on GST.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is so that we can look to raise and improve the job prospects of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Member Mr Pritam Singh for this clarification.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What the Member has said is felt by all of us.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Let us work together, let us make the workplace, let us make work, let us make job quality our priority, and let us make work satisfying to as many people as possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: I was heartened to hear that retirement adequacy is improving rapidly for the current generation of workers, and for women in particular.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: But I think we are both still concerned about the retirement adequacy of women who spend significant amounts of time out of the labour force.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: So, can we study ways to more formally recognise the contributions that they are making towards strengthening our families, for example, through CPF credits for caregiving?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: This year's Budget has already given top-ups which are targeted more or less at such women, and we already spend considerable amounts of money on tax relief for working women.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: So, we can possibly do more for women who are out of the labour force and who are doing important work at home.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chairman, I believe that there was a Motion on Caregivers and I am not sure whether this subject was discussed then.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We, of course, already have tax incentives to encourage cash top-ups and made it easier for members to transfer their CPF savings to their spouses, parents and grandparents, many of whom are women.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, in this way, we hope to help the women build up their retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There is one datapoint that is quite useful.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We looked at the members who received top-ups, and after they received the top-ups, they reached the Basic Retirement Sum.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: First of all, I would like to thank the Senior Parliamentary Secretary for sharing on the progress of FWAs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Beyond just offering FWAs, from the employee’s point of view, from the businesses’ as well, what efforts are being done to help them better leverage FWAs in the totality of the new work arrangements that we are seeing, beyond just offering flexbile work, but really in the way workspaces are used, in the way technologies are used, because there are lots of effort in helping companies be productive, and also getting more productivity from the workers?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And in line with that, new skills that workers need to thrive in this new environment as well as the terms under which work then gets measured and also protected.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Chairman, I want to thank the Member Ms Jessica Tan for her passion on this topic and her clarifications.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Earlier on, I did mention that, currently, our female employment rate is high.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We ranked 7th out of 36 OECD countries.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Even though there are now more women in the workforce, MOM will not let up in our efforts to enhance the support system.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Actually, you really need a whole ecosystem to work to help women better balance our work and also family responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The first one, I spoke extensively about FWAs, and it is not just about Work-Life Grant.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: It is also about sharing with employers how it is also win-win.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: There are actually three ways to look at FWAs.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I think Ms Jessica Tan is quite familiar with that.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Some mothers will say that they have to whip up lunch for their kids.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: So, they work out an arrangement with their boss for them to come in at 10.00 am.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: But they will stay back till about seven o'clock.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: An example of flexi-load is job-sharing where we want to focus a bit more effort because it involves job redesign, sometimes also workplace redesign.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This is where Ms Jessica Tan is absolutely correct.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We heard very good updates on SEPs, especially the fact that it is not growing and that many are still in the traditional sector.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Is that a concern for MOM and is this a growing trend?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Is it an indication there is underemployment or is this an interim transitional thing?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chairman, my observation is that I have seen some of these Deliveroo, Grab Eats service people.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And when I have asked, they are taking this on to earn some pocket money.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I have also seen some other people do this on weekends.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When I have asked them, not all of them are doing it on a full-time basis; some of them are earning something extra.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In terms of boosting a person's income, in terms of giving him options, if that is what our individual wishes to do, they certainly should be entitled to decide for themselves.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will have to continue to monitor the trends.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As it is, as the Member pointed out again that the SEP numbers went down.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I would be very concerned if the numbers grew very quickly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As it looks right now, over all, the numbers have not changed.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One other thing that we have noticed, and I shared with the House last year, is that SEPs are quite flexible.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There were occasions where we noticed that people had chosen to switch into driving private hire cars because the incomes that they got was better than, for example, selling real estate, because the real estate market is quieter.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, there is some movement amongst the different occupations within self-employment.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: But would the Minister consider lowering the PEA and let the member decide, because the tradeoff, if you have an early withdrawal, you are going to get less, and if you delay your withdrawal, you are going to get more?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Workers' Party has called for it previously and the Government has also taken pains to explain what the considerations are.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Essentially, it is to do with extended longevity and also being mindful of what other countries are doing.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, I happened to have addressed this question quite recently in Parliament, and my answer has not changed.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, with your permission, Mr Chairman, I suggest we move on.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But Mr Png actually also made some other references to CPF in his earlier cut.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chairman, I wonder if you would allow me to address them since I did not have time to address them earlier?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Actually, Mr Png Eng Huat compared CPF savings to something like a fixed deposit (FD), meaning whenever you want, you should be able to take it out.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: At the end of your maturity date, you should be able to take out with interest.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At the end of the maturity date, you should be able to take it out with interest?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When the member is about to reach 65, we remind him.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Then we write to him again and we remind him, year after year.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, Mr Png, which bank will you be more happy with?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The one that rolls over for you automatically because it earns more, or the one that quickly terminates it and let it earn less?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Chairman, my question is for the Minister of State Zaqy Mohamad.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am glad that MOM will encourage building owners to provide rest areas for outsourced workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But the reality is that many building owners, they need to carve out existing areas to be rest areas, and this would involve increasing their gross floor area, and there will be a developmental charge.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am proposing, maybe in his capacity in MND, to consider waiving this developmental charge for areas, if it is being carved out, to be rest areas.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I believe that should be an MND cut though.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But having said that, it is good that Members are concerned with this area.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But as I have mentioned at the start, we will start with cleaners first because we know that it is the right thing to do.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But it is not going to be easy for everyone.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, that is why even for hawker centres, we start with the new ones first.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And the old ones, as they retrofit, they upgrade, we will work with NEA to see how we can provide those.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And, certainly, for buildings, I can also understand some of the difficulties.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: This may be more a question of updating our workplace health and safety to embrace total health and safety that includes psychosocial well-being because we are already doing it.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: But the WSH Act is still very much skewed towards physical health and safety.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Could the Minister please give clarification on that?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: At this moment, we do a lot of promotional work around mental well-being.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, I am not sure exactly which aspect of WSH does the Member want to include that in.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But a lot of the work we do today looks at safety issues, occupational diseases.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, if the Member is specific in the areas that she thinks we could work on, we are happy to work with her and consult her on it.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: I have two clarification questions for the Minister.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: I asked that question because I take $700 as what is deemed sufficient.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: The second clarification question is: the good thing about this group of seniors is that 76% of them have property.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Therefore, it is very important when CPF talks with them about planning, they can speak about unlocking value in the property.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: I know probably it is not immediately in the remit of CPF.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: So, I would like to ask how would that be addressed in helping them to understand the value in their property if they want a much more comfortable retirement and they wanted to unlock that value.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, there is room for these kinds of services to be improved.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But it appears to us that quite a lot of people also feel that they have the knowledge and they are quite confident about making decisions for themselves.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The question is, are there people who would benefit from such services but are not aware that they are being offered?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, that is an area we need to work on.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Patrick Tay, would you like to withdraw your amendment?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: If I may just sum up in three tag lines after hearing the last four-and-a-half hours of sharing.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I think the first tag line is we want our workers to be not just employed, employable but also empowered, engaged and equally treated.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: And for employers to embrace transformation before transformation embraces them.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: And, finally, every worker matters and every tripartite partner matters, too.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: So, on that note, I would also like to place on record my thanks to Permanent Secretary Aubeck Kam, Deputy Secretaries Poon Hong Yuen and Augustin Lee, CPF Board Chief Executive Ng Chee Peng as well as WSG Chief Executive Tan Choon Shian, and the entire MOM team powering this COS, and, of course, my fellow Members of this House who have contributed in all their cuts and all the clarifications.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: On that note, I beg leave to withdraw my amendment.
